claims.text: The target material is a multiphase AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5-type high-entropy alloy.
The alloy has distinct interpenetrating eutectic phases.
Protective passive oxide layers form naturally at the phase boundaries of the target alloy at elevated temperature.
High-temperature oxidation produces a protective oxide layer preferentially along eutectic phase boundaries.
Mechanical abrasion cyclically removes or disrupts the oxide film during simultaneous wear and corrosion.
Cyclic oxide disruption repeatedly exposes fresh reactive metal at eutectic interfaces.
Potential differences between phases can create localized galvanic cells and accelerate selective dissolution at phase boundaries.
Localized passive-film breakdown can expose the alloy matrix and promote pitting corrosion.
Localized galvanic corrosion and pitting at phase boundaries undermine adjacent phases' structural integrity and wear resistance.
Wear exposes additional surface area to corrosion, producing an accelerating positive feedback loop between wear and corrosion.
A protective oxide layer improves the elevated-temperature wear resistance of AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 under atmospheric conditions.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will cause synergistically greater total degradation than the wear-only and corrosion-only conditions.
The simultaneous condition will produce deeper and more irregular wear tracks than the wear-only baseline.
The simultaneous condition will produce more localized pitting than the corrosion-only baseline.
Oxide-film formation and removal cycles will correlate temporally with increased damage.
The proposed mechanism requires approximately 500 °C, sufficient oxygen for oxide formation, chloride ions, and mechanical loading capable of disrupting the oxide.
Wear-only testing in inert argon and static corrosion-only immersion provide controls for the simultaneous tribocorrosion condition.
Absence of oxide-layer fluctuations coupled to pitting and enhanced wear, or observation of merely additive degradation, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
